title: Mint-Agent: Introducing Finance-Native Agentic Foundation Models
abstract: Financial agents must do more than recall domain knowledge: they must be both reliable, executing precise operations over grounded evidence, and executive, sustaining long-horizon research whose conclusions remain auditable. We present Mint-Agent, a family of finance-native agentic models designed around these two scales of financial intelligence. Mint-Agent is built upon three pillars: data, harness, and algorithm. Our data engine constructs clean, specialized tasks for atomic financial capabilities and long-horizon agentic execution from real-world financial sources. MintHarness enables stable interaction with open-ended environments and maintains auditable evidence trails across extended research trajectories. Our training recipe combines SFT, critical-step OPD, and RLVR to develop separate financial reasoning and agentic execution experts, which are then unified through model merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation into compact, general-purpose financial agents. This pipeline yields two flagship models, Mint-Cu (9B) and Mint-Ag (27B). Across professional financial benchmarks, our models demonstrate two defining strengths: (1) Reliability: Mint-Ag achieves 98.33% on RFC-Bench, surpassing GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-4.8 by 3.66 and 3.00 points; and (2) Executability: Mint-Cu reaches 69.86% on FinSearchComp T2, outperforming Agents-A1-35B and Nex-N2-mini by 22.83 and 12.78 points, while Mint-Ag achieves 76.00% and 60.49% on FinanceAgentBench v1.1 and v2, respectively. These results establish a path toward trustworthy financial intelligence in which domain expertise, long-horizon execution, and auditable evidence are jointly engineered as a unified foundation for frontier agentic models.
why: Finance agents with auditable trails; actual deployment unknown.

title: zLend: A Dual-Scope Cash-Flow Reconstruction Framework for On-Chain Credit Underwriting
abstract: Decentralized lending lacks a credit bureau: a borrower's capacity to repay must be inferred entirely from public on-chain activity, without income verification or a liability record. This paper presents zLend, a deployed cash-flow underwriting framework that reconstructs a wallet's daily balance history from raw token transfers and derives short-duration repayment-capacity signals from it. The reconstruction is performed twice per wallet, once restricted to a fixed stablecoin basket and once over all fungible transfers, on the premise that a wallet's total token holdings and its liquid, spendable balance are distinct quantities whose conflation misprices risk. From each series we derive liquidity coverage against a fixed loan size, cash-flow volatility and regularity, a drawdown-and-recovery statistic adapted from quantitative finance, and a recurring-counterparty detector that identifies salary-like payment cadence from transfer timing alone. The two views are then compared: a wallet with large aggregate holdings whose stablecoin reserve rarely covers the loan size is flagged as a liquidity mismatch irrespective of total wealth. We specify the pipeline formally, document the golden-master methodology used to verify a cross-language production migration to numerical tolerance 1e-9, and characterize the tier function's parameter sensitivity with an independent reimplementation validated to exact agreement (78 of 78 field assertions) against the deployed system's reference fixtures. Tier assignment is governed predominantly by the reference loan size, with four of six reference wallets changing tier across loan sizes from USD 10 to USD 25,000; the drawdown and coverage criteria bind on disjoint wallets, so neither subsumes the other; and no criterion in the tier rule is inert. zLend is deployed in production, informing real lending decisions via third-party API integrations.
why: Deployed on-chain credit underwriting framework, specific technical innovations.

title: AccountAgent: AI Accounting Assistant System
abstract: The AI Accounting Assistant System is an innovative tool that improves the accuracy and efficiency of financial management and is becoming a core support for enterprise accounting. It relies on machine learning, natural language processing, and data visualization to automate the full accounting agent including bookkeeping, report generation, and data analysis, substantially reducing manual operations and minimizing human error. Designed to resolve the pain points of low efficiency, cumbersome workflows, and data lag in traditional accounting, the system shifts financial work from repetitive labor toward high-value decision support. It deeply mines historical financial data, precisely identifies operating trends, and provides real-time, targeted insight for strategic planning, risk prevention, and operating decisions. By reconstructing the accounting agent, the system realizes automated bookkeeping, intelligent analysis, and efficient compliance, driving the accounting profession from a bookkeeping orientation toward a management orientation. This document presents the architecture, methodology, key algorithms, and functional modules of the platform.
why: Accounting automation, off-topic for financial research.

title: LAVA: Logic-Aware Validation and Augmentation Framework for Large-Scale Financial Document Auditing
abstract: Financial document validation in production, such as payroll auditing, tax compliance, and loan underwriting, demands exceptional accuracy, consistency, and reproducibility under strict enterprise constraints. In practice, documents arrive with heterogeneous layouts and formats, semantically rich and context-dependent content, and embedded business rules that current pipelines struggle to process reliably. We introduce LAVA (Logic-Aware Validation and Augmentation), a modular, backbone-agnostic pipeline built on multimodal large language models, that integrates a four-stage design: document-rule retrieval, layout-preserving information extraction, auxiliary metadata enrichment, and auditable symbolic/arithmetic verification. LAVA supports robust rule grounding, fine-grained error attribution, and consistent, traceable end-to-end execution, capabilities essential for high-stakes deployment. Evaluated on a large real-world benchmark with diverse financial documents and dozens of expert-curated validation rules, LAVA outperforms baselines in hallucination control and edge-case handling while maintaining efficient token usage, demonstrating practicality for high-volume, time-critical validation.
why: Multimodal LLM document auditing; unproven deployment.

title: Synthesizing Feature Extractors: An Agentic Approach for Algorithm Selection
abstract: Algorithm selection for constraint satisfaction problems requires extracting features that capture problem structure. Manually designing feature extractors demands deep domain expertise and quickly becomes a bottleneck when new problem classes appear. We present an automated approach that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) in an agentic check--fix--verify loop to synthesize executable Python scripts that act as interpretable, problem-specific feature extractors. Given a high-level MiniZinc model and an instance, the LLM agent generates code that constructs a typed graph representation and computes structural properties such as graph density, variable clustering, and constraint tightness. We evaluate our approach on three combinatorial problems (vehicle routing, car sequencing, fixed-length error-correcting codes) with a portfolio of five state-of-the-art solvers. The synthesized extractors yield algorithm selectors that consistently outperform both expert-curated mzn2feat features (up to $8.3$ percentage points (pp) test-set accuracy on FLECC) and the best transformer-based trans2feat variants. In the meanwhile, the synthesized feature extractors remain inspectable.
why: Off-topic: constraint-satisfaction algorithm selection.

title: ALPS: Measuring Valid Creativity in Large Language Models with Mathematical Construction
abstract: Large language models produce outputs presented as discoveries - new proofs, conjectures, or molecules. Whether such an output that appears creative is truly original and effective is hard to establish: open-ended outputs require subjective judgment, the output may replicate something seen in training, or the task may be too simple to need creativity. We present ALPS (Austin-Law Proof-Synthesis), a benchmark that designs a task to measure valid creativity: producing a solution that is original and can be proven correct. Each instance is a single equational law, certified to require either the construction of an infinite mathematical structure satisfying the law, or a proof that no such structure exists. Submissions are verified by automated proof checking with no human involvement, and a public generator produces new instances without limit, so LLMs are never evaluated on problems they may have seen. A portfolio of eight configurations of leading automated provers resolves 2.2% of the 4,141-law evaluation pool, and a twentyfold budget increase adds 0.6%: the obstacle is not compute, but the absence of any method that produces the tailored structure each law requires. Under a fixed protocol, the strongest reasoning model we test succeeds in 14% of instances on the proof side, but none on the construction side. The remaining 97.2% of the pool is unresolved at every configuration and budget we test. We release ALPS in full: the corpus, the generator, and the automated judge.
why: Off-topic: mathematical theorem creativity benchmarks.

title: Governance at the Boundary: How Agent Decomposition Degrades Policy Compliance
abstract: Existing agent benchmarks ask whether the agent finished the task. We ask whether it finished it within policy. We introduce Fiducia-bench, a benchmark for the governability of financial agents---whether they escalate when obligated, abstain when required, and leave an auditable trail---and use it to study a question no prior benchmark addresses: does decomposing an agent into components degrade its governance? It does, and the mechanism is specific. Policy-relevant facts discovered by one component are attenuated at the handoff boundary before reaching the component that must act on them. In a 626-episode experiment across 100 KYC/AML task variants, two models, and three architectures, a 32B open-weights model attenuated 0% of discovered facts under a single-loop baseline, 56% under a fixed pipeline, and 85% under an orchestrator-subagent architecture (all at constraint distance 2). A stronger model (gpt-4.1-mini) attenuated 3-6% under the same conditions, suggesting the governance cost of decomposition is partly a function of model capability. Critically, the same mechanism produces both under-escalation and over-escalation, depending on whether the dropped fact was a risk signal or an exculpating one. The benchmark, all tasks, and the verification harness are open-source
why: Decomposed agents lose 56-85% policy-relevant facts at boundaries.

title: Dynamic Regime-Aware Conformal Calibration for Reliable Economic Forecast Intervals under Multiple Distribution Shifts
abstract: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free prediction intervals but relies on exchangeability, an assumption often violated in economic forecasting because of covariate shift, concept drift, local heterogeneity and latent regimes. We propose Dynamic Regime-Aware Conformal Prediction (DRACP), which combines density-ratio, localized kernel and probabilistic regime-aware weighting with a self-tuning online significance controller in a unified weighted conformal calibration framework. We distinguish three theoretical results: finite-sample validity under oracle importance weights, a coverage-gap bound for estimated weights with rates in effective sample size, and deterministic or regret guarantees for the online controller. We evaluate DRACP against six baselines on 48 real forecasting series covering euro-area and EU-27 HICP inflation, US macroeconomic and energy indicators, and daily financial series. Recent online methods (FACI, strongly-adaptive online conformal prediction and conformal PID) were verified against the authors' implementations. DRACP is not the most efficient method: strongly-adaptive online conformal prediction achieves the best interval score and intervals about 20% narrower. Instead, DRACP provides the most reliable calibration, achieving coverage closest to the nominal 0.90 (0.890), never falling below 0.80 on any series, maintaining the best coverage at all forecast horizons, and performing best during the 2021-2023 inflation surge. The strongly-adaptive method undercovers on 20 of 48 series versus 10 for DRACP. DRACP therefore offers a principled trade-off between calibration and efficiency, favoring reliable coverage when prediction intervals must satisfy coverage standards. An ablation study shows that the online controller and conditional-scale normalization provide most of the performance gain, whereas the weighting components make a smaller contribution.
why: Conformal calibration under drift; solid but no advantage shown.

title: What Do Compliance Detectors Read? An Audit of Activation Probes and Guard Models
abstract: Regulatory compliance monitoring in deployed language models is increasingly implemented as a legal and audit control, checking model outputs against written rules spanning data protection, healthcare, financial regulation, and platform policy. Such monitoring is meaningful only if a detector's verdict depends on the stated rule rather than on surface features of the scenario. We show this condition fails across the current class of compliance detectors, a failure we call rule blindness. Deleting, permuting, or substituting the governing rule leaves detection accuracy unchanged for every guard and activation probe we test, including a policy-conditioned guard that correctly cites the governing clause yet barely changes its verdict when that clause is swapped for its permissive counterpart. A purpose-built benchmark crossing two rules with two scenarios, so that neither alone predicts the label, confirms the failure under a design no prior benchmark rules out, and shows that step by step reasoning, not any fast detector we test, is what escapes it. Auditing at scale requires a retraining-free detector, so we introduce the Internal Compliance Score (ICS): a training-free activation readout calibrated from ten labelled pairs and scored by a single projection. We hold ICS to the same scrutiny as the guards it audits: a pre-registered criterion for beating trivial baselines is not met, and a bag-of-words model matches its pooled generalisation exactly. It remains useful because it is inexpensive, letting us audit four deployed guard models, an 8B zero-shot judge, and thirteen benchmarks, and it raises the mechanically verified pass rate when used to rank candidate responses, though an adaptive white-box attack removes this gain. We release the counterfactual protocol and crossed-rule benchmark so rule blindness can be tested in future probe and guard claims.
why: Compliance detectors exhibit rule-blindness across all tested systems.

title: When ratios fall: A dynamic approach to contingent convertibles
abstract: We propose a novel valuation framework for contingent convertible (CoCo) bonds based on the issuing bank's Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio, which is widely acknowledged as an indicator of a bank's solvency. Our approach develops a bivariate jump-diffusion model that captures the dynamic relationship linking the CET1 ratios, share prices, and CoCo bond prices, incorporating both continuous market movements and correlated jump risk. The model advances existing literature through three key innovations: (1) a hybrid mechanism for modeling regulatory discretion in trigger decisions, (2) a class of power conversion schemes that generalizes traditional approaches while maintaining analytical tractability, and (3) a method to overcome the temporal discrepancy between high-frequency market data and low-frequency regulatory reporting. We derive semi-closed form formulas for both write-down and equity-convertible CoCo bonds and validate our model through five case studies spanning from 2009 to 2023, including an in-depth analysis of the 2023 Credit Suisse collapse. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in pricing and hedging performance while highlighting the model's data-adaptive nature that enables short-term predictions.
why: CoCo bond pricing theory; pure theory, no data deployment.

title: Rough Volatility Across Assets
abstract: We measure volatility roughness across asset classes using a common data infrastructure and pipeline. Our data covers 3,926 United States equities, 34 CME futures roots, rates, FX, and commodities, and options on 44 underlyings over 2010-2025. Realized volatility is rough everywhere. The class-median Hurst estimate ranges from $0.05$ (livestock) through $0.07-0.10$ (rates, FX, agriculture, energy, metals) to $0.13$ (single stocks) and $0.20$ (equity indices). The option-implied measure identifies $H$ only where the leverage effect produces a clean skew term structure. For the equity indices, implied estimates of $0.21-0.28$ are just above realized volatility $H$, while for rates and FX the ATM skew regression fails with an R-squared near zero even though realized volatility remains rough. We also show a mean-reversion contamination formula for the second-moment estimator of the roughness for the stationary fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. The local slope of the increment second moment deviates from $2H$ by $(1-H)Γ(2H+1)(κΔ)^{2-2H}$ for all $H\in(0,1)$. A correction framework for the second moment, when the log realized volatility measure has additive noise, raised the $H$ estimate slightly but nowhere near the Brownian diffusion framework. Finally, a failure taxonomy discusses where rough-volatility methods apply and where they fail, suggesting alternative paths to further explore the rough-volatility paradigm.
why: Rough volatility measured across 3,926 equities and major assets.

title: Bayesian Volatility Modelling and Machine Learning Forecasting in Global Energy and Agricultural Commodity Markets: A Probabilistic Framework for Dynamic Dependence Analysis
abstract: Forecasting the dynamic relationships among commodity markets is essential for effective portfolio management, risk diversification, and policy formulation. This study examines the volatility dynamics and time-varying dependence between global energy and agricultural commodity markets by integrating Bayesian stochastic volatility (SV) modelling, the Dynamic Conditional Correlation (DCC) model, and machine learning forecasting techniques. Daily returns for Brent crude oil, natural gas, wheat, corn, and soybean from January 2010 to December 2025 were analyzed. The Bayesian SV model was employed to estimate latent volatility, while the DCC model captured the evolving conditional correlations among commodity returns. The resulting dynamic correlations were subsequently forecast using Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models. Forecast performance was evaluated using the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and the Diebold-Mariano test. The findings reveal persistent time-varying volatility across all commodity markets and stronger dynamic dependence among agricultural commodities than between energy and agricultural markets. Among the competing forecasting models, XGBoost achieved the highest predictive accuracy, outperforming both Random Forest and LSTM across all evaluation metrics. The Diebold-Mariano test further confirmed that the forecasting improvements of XGBoost were statistically significant. These findings demonstrate that combining Bayesian stochastic volatility modelling with machine learning techniques provides a robust framework for modelling and forecasting dynamic commodity market dependence, offering valuable insights for investors, portfolio managers, and policymakers in commodity risk management.
why: Standard Bayesian-SV-DCC-ML ensemble; no performance comparison baseline.

title: Beyond the Representative Agent: Causal Machine Learning for Heterogeneous Household Responses to Monetary Policy in the Euro Area
abstract: Monetary policy transmission is heterogeneous across households, yet the analytical toolkit of central banks remains anchored in average effects and a small set of hand-picked conditioning variables. This manuscript identifies and articulates the gap between the causal machine learning frontier and the practice of monetary policy analysis in the euro area, and proposes a comprehensive framework for estimating the full distribution of household-level responses to monetary policy and converting it into distributional impact assessment. The empirical literature has established that consumption responses to interest rate changes are concentrated among specific household types — mortgagors in the United Kingdom and the United States, and households with high liquid wealth and floating-rate debt in Norway — and that contractionary monetary policy systematically raises income and consumption inequality. The theoretical literature has established, through heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models, that the distribution of balance sheets shapes aggregate transmission. What neither literature provides is a systematic method for recovering the conditional average treatment effect function of a monetary policy shock across the full covariate space of household balance sheets, income, demographics, and expectations — the object that causal forests, double/debiased machine learning, and policy learning are designed to deliver. The framework developed here integrates (i) credible high frequency identification of euro area monetary policy shocks, (ii) harmonized household micro data from the Eurosystem Household Finance and Consumption Survey and Bundesbank research data infrastructure, (iii) causal machine learning estimators adapted to the time-series structure of macro shocks, and (iv) a distributional impact assessment protocol aligned with the European Central Bank's post-2021 strategy framework. Policy implications for the Eurosystem, the German Bundesbank, and European macroprudential and fiscal policy are developed, including the use of estimated heterogeneity to design targeted compensatory measures and to improve aggregate projections by aggregating micro responses. The manuscript is anchored in verified funding architecture — ERC, DFG, the Excellence Strategy, and Horizon Europe — and is written to Q1 journal standards in American English with APA 7 citation practice.
why: Heterogeneous monetary policy responses framework; methodology only, no results.

title: A Survey of Simulation in Finance: Data, Methods, Applications, and Evaluation
abstract: Simulation has long been an important tool in finance, from Monte Carlo pricing and risk analysis to artificial markets and agent-based models. Recent advances in high-frequency data, reinforcement learning, deep generative models, and large language model (LLM) agents have substantially expanded the scope of financial simulation. Contemporary studies no longer use simulation only to approximate price paths or evaluate portfolios; they increasingly construct interactive market environments, synthetic limit order books, heterogeneous trading populations, user simulators, and multi-agent financial decision systems. This survey reviews the emerging literature on simulation in finance through four dimensions: the financial problems being simulated, the datasets and environments used to support simulation, the methodological paradigms adopted by existing studies, and the evaluation protocols used to assess realism and performance. Based on a structured review table covering market simulators, agent-based models, LLM-based financial agents, reinforcement-learning environments, and generative market models, we propose a taxonomy of financial simulation research and identify major open challenges, including benchmark fragmentation, limited data availability, simulation-to-reality gaps, and the difficulty of evaluating agent behavior in complex financial systems.
why: Survey of financial simulation; reader rejects literature reviews.

title: Does Generative AI Increase Investment Convergence?
abstract: This paper investigates convergence in investor behavior driven by the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in finance, exemplified by the introduction of ChatGPT in 2022. Using a recently developed measure of investor reliance on GenAI information, difference-indifferences estimations indicate that the positive relationship between fund reliance on GenAI and portfolio similarity strengthens following the introduction of ChatGPT. The effect is more pronounced for firms with higher common ownership and richer information environments. While firms more exposed to GenAI-reliant funds exhibit an accelerated speed of price discovery, they also experience a notable reduction in stock-level liquidity. This liquidity decline is most pronounced among firms with high common ownership and transparent information environments. Collectively, the findings reveal an underexplored channel through which deployment of GenAI tools may influence financial market outcomes.
why: GenAI adoption causes fund convergence and liquidity degradation.

title: The Latency Frontier: Mapping the Limits of Financial Observability
abstract: The non-bank financial intermediation sector reached $256.8 trillion in assets in 2024 — 51.0 percent of global financial assets — with private credit alone approaching $2 trillion globally, much of it outside the disclosure regimes governing public markets. Private credit and private equity funds typically report valuations quarterly, on a model-derived basis, rather than continuously. The canonical contagion framework, Eisenberg and Noe (2001), assumes a network's obligations and asset values are fully observable. Mark-to-model reporting violates that assumption structurally: a fund can be insolvent in fact while solvent in every observable record until its next scheduled valuation. This paper formalises that condition as a zombie node, and the interval of non-disclosure as a latency wedge, δᵢ(t). This paper develops the Granger-Augmented Latency Estimator (GALE), an extension of the Eisenberg-Noe clearing framework: the same fixed-point clearing map evaluated at a corrected input, not a separate procedure placed beside it. GALE estimates the unobservable latency wedge from market behaviour in publicly traded instruments linked to a private fund — BDC equity, regional bank CDS, short-interest and borrow-fee data — without requiring compelled disclosure of private fund positions. Five subordinate modules extend the baseline estimator, each with an explicit point where it stops working: GALE-K (a state-space filter for delayed or obscured proxy data), GALE-N (a cross-dealer test for exposure fragmentation and circular evergreening), GALE-CB (a covariance-bridging estimator for cases lacking historical depth), GALE-V (Implied Synthetic Volatility, reversing mark-to-model smoothing via liquid credit proxies), and GALE-P (projecting the estimate forward into probability, timing, magnitude, and systemic footprint of a future breach). The mechanism is examined against six cases: two historical episodes where a public proxy signal preceded official recognition of distress (Wirecard, 2016–2020; First Brands and Tricolor, 2025); one, Archegos (2021), where proxy estimation reaches a rank-deficient identification limit; one live, unresolved case — AI-infrastructure private-credit financing, flagged by the BIS in June 2026 — extending the framework prospectively; and two executable numerical tests, the March 2020 Ares Capital contraction (a full-information baseline) and the March 2023 SVB collapse (testing the state-space extension under degraded data). A panel VAR specification, policy recommendations scoped to existing legal authority, and a comparative survey of four regulatory regimes complete the analysis.
why: Private credit mark-to-model gap formalized; validation pending.

title: Requisite Variety and Observability: Value-Creation-Chain Tokenization and Artificial Intelligence in the Architecture of Financial Regulation
abstract: This paper continues the author's research program on the tokenization of the value creation chain based on the SDA (Structured Digital Assets) methodology: Korabayev (2026a) introduced the formal methodology and the five-level trust architecture, while Korabayev (2026b) demonstrated its systemic effects empirically on a three-module simulationincluding an increase in the transparency of the entire processing chain. The author provides this empirically established transparency effect with a rigorous theoretical foundation. The difficulty of contemporary financial regulation is interpreted not as a crisis of a particular monetary model but as a structural requisite-variety gap between the complexity of the real production-and-logistics sector and the observational-and-computational capacity of the supervisory apparatus. The gap is formalized through W. R. Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety and the Touchette-Lloyd information-theoretic limit of control; it is stated explicitly that this is a heuristic transposition of the principle into entropic language, not a proven theorem for economic systems. It is argued that tokenization combined with artificial intelligence forms a two-sided mechanism for closing the gap: tokenization and technical oracles raise observability (the mutual information between the controlled system and the regulator), while AI raises the computational capacity of the regulator, which by the Conant-Ashby theorem must embody a model of the controlled system. A two-level anchor-modular architecture is proposed. The limits of the approach are stated honestly: the oracle problem is not eliminated but compressed to a smaller, more costly, and more observable residue; requisite variety is a necessary but not a sufficient condition.
why: Regulatory requisite-variety theory; position paper, no implementation path.

title: Theory of Algorithmic Financial Cognition (TAFC): Mitigating the Epistemic Risk of Algorithmic Homogeneity in Global Markets
abstract: The evolution of global financial markets from human-led environments to autonomous algorithmic ecosystems constitutes a significant structural transformation. While post-2008 macroprudential regulations, culminating in Basel IV, strengthened capital and liquidity requirements, they fail to address a newly emergent, unpriced structural vulnerability: Algorithmic Homogeneity. As tier-one financial institutions increasingly deploy identically trained Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) relying on shared foundational architectures and commoditized data, cognitive diversity in the market is severely diminished. During periods of significant market stress, this convergence produces "Synchronized Liquidity Shocks" where algorithmic agents collectively withdraw liquidity or execute unidirectional trades, rendering traditional capital buffers functionally insufficient. This paper introduces the Theory of Algorithmic Financial Cognition (TAFC), an intellectual framework that reclassifies AI systems from IT infrastructure to autonomous cognitive entities ("Synthetic Market Actors"). Furthermore, it operationalizes this theory by introducing the Salih Index for Algorithmic Diversity (SIAD), a novel tripartite vector methodology designed to quantify convergence in input data, structural topology, and behavioral outputs among algorithmic participants. By integrating the SIAD into global regulatory standards, policymakers can implement a proactive Cognitive Capital Surcharge (CCS) to penalize herd behavior, incentivize algorithmic diversity, and restore Cognitive Sovereignty over global financial ecosystems.
why: Algorithmic homogeneity as systemic risk; concern-raising only, no solution.

title: A Hybrid Machine Learning and Rule-Based Decision Support System for Short-Term Trading: A Case Study on XAUUSD
abstract: Financial markets, characterized by high liquidity and rapid capital flows, require reliable predictive tools to support trading decisions and risk management. This study evaluates several machine learning algorithms to identify a robust short-term price forecasting model and, based on these findings, develops a rule-based decision-support system for algorithmic trading. Using XGBoost with tailored feature engineering, the proposed model forecasts five-minute gold (XAU/USD) price movements over a one-hour horizon, achieving a root mean square error (RMSE) of 3.49 and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 0.11%. When operationalized as a complete trading strategy governed by a fixed-dollar-risk position-sizing rule, the system produced a cumulative net return of 130.62% ($13,062.38 profit on a $10,000 initial capital) over the January 2021-October 2025 period, with Monte Carlo simulation indicating a mean annualized return of approximately 30.7% and an 89% probability of annual profitability. These results highlight the model's effectiveness for data-driven investment and automated trading applications.
why: XAUUSD backtest 130% gain, no transaction costs, overfitted.

title: AI-Driven Business Transformation: Automation, Productivity, Employment, and the Emergence of the Agentic Enterprise A Literature-Grounded Conceptual and Empirical Study, With a Bounded Pre-AI Baseline From the World Bank FAT India Survey
abstract: Generative AI and increasingly agentic AI systems are being adopted into business operations far faster than the academic literature on their organizational consequences is being produced, creating a persistent gap between what is claimed in industry discourse and what is empirically established. This paper synthesizes the credible empirical and theoretical literature on AIdriven business transformation — spanning task-level productivity experiments (Noy & Zhang, 2023; Peng, Kalliamvakou, Cihon, & Demirer, 2023; Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; Brynjolfsson, Li, & Raymond, 2025), labor-economics frameworks for automation (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2019), occupational-exposure studies (Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin, & Rock, 2024; Cazzaniga et al., 2024), and early evidence on small-business impacts (Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz, & Koning, 2025) — to address the question: how is AI transforming business operations, productivity, decision-making, employment, and competitive advantage, and what risks and limitations accompany that transformation? The paper develops two original conceptual contributions, explicitly identified as such rather than as established literature: a seven-level Automation Maturity Model distinguishing rule-based automation from generative, agentic, and increasingly autonomous business processes; and a six-level Human-Oversight Spectrum for governing the autonomy businesses grant AI systems. It systematically reviews AI’s differential impact across nine business functions, evaluates six research propositions against the assembled evidence (finding strong support for task-level over job-level automation and for complementary-capability dependence, and only partial, evidence-thin support for claims about small-business democratization), and presents a risk and governance framework spanning technical, business, security, legal, organizational, and socioeconomic dimensions. As a bounded empirical complement — not the paper’s central evidence base — the paper incorporates a validated analysis of the World Bank’s Firm Adoption of Technology (FAT) Survey for India, which measures pre-generative-AI technology sophistication among 1,519 formal establishments in Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh; this survey cannot measure AI adoption directly (documented in detail) but its finding that technology sophistication already varies sharply by firm size and technical human capital is used to inform, not substitute for, the paper’s argument about which businesses are best positioned for AI-era transformation. The paper closes with practical implications for the design of AI systems intended to automate meaningful portions of SMB operations while preserving appropriate human oversight, and is explicit throughout about the boundary between literature findings, the one bounded empirical analysis, original conceptual framework, and author inference.
why: Business transformation and AI employment survey; off-topic for reader.

title: Automation, Income Incidence, and Capital Accumulation in Incomplete Markets
abstract: This paper studies how automation changes the stationary distribution of income, consumption, and wealth in an incomplete-market economy. An automating sector trades off productivity gains and labor-cost savings against adoption costs. Households differ by skill and wealth, save in a capital/equity claim, and face uninsurable skill risk. Competitive factor prices and aggregate capital clear jointly with household Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations and the stationary Kolmogorov forward equation. Automation affects consumption through labor-income incidence, precautionary saving, skill mobility, ownership of automation rents, and the stationary capital stock. In an adverseincidence scenario with high exposure, adverse reskilling, capital obsolescence, and concentrated ownership, decentralized automation lowers stationary consumption and capital relative to the no-automation allocation. With stronger productivity and complementarity, lower obsolescence, and broader ownership, automation raises output, consumption, and capital. Reversing the assumed skillmobility response also raises consumption, output, and capital substantially at a fixed automation intensity. A proxy diagnostic combining U.S. evidence on AI adoption, investment, labor-income pass-through, equity ownership, and marginal propensities to consume places the current economy near the boundary between the two scenarios. The model provides a quantitative framework for separating automation’s aggregate gains from its distributional incidence.
why: Automation's income distribution in theory; no empirical validation.

title: The Fallback as Signal: Preserved Human Skill, Liability, and Competence Signaling in Credence-Good Markets under Improving AI
abstract: Firms that deploy improving but imperfect AI must decide how much to keep human workers engaged. Engagement lowers current output yet builds the fallback skill the firm needs when AI fails. We ask what that fallback skill signals to two audiences at once: mobile workers, who sort across firms on the skill trajectory a job builds, and clients, who cannot observe skill in a credence-good market and must infer competence. We embed the engagement-skill dynamics of Singh et al. (2026) in a signaling game and add a liability commitment. Because a more-skilled provider fails less often precisely in the states where AI is down, the expected cost of a liability pledge is decreasing in fallback skill. This restores Spence-Mirrlees single crossing on a type that is endogenous-built, not drawnand yields a separating equilibrium in which liability certifies preserved human competence that no artifact can certify once AI writes as well as the expert. We characterize the least-cost separating pledge schedule, show that client stakes shift engagement toward or away from the least-skilled worker depending on the size of the pledge, and derive a stakes threshold above which building skill dominates free-riding on a rival's training-reversing the asymmetric-specialization result of the underlying labor model. Two boundaries close the market from both sides: small tickets cannot fund enforcement, and large tickets exceed the provider's solvency. An agent-based version of the market reproduces the analytical thresholds under noisy beliefs, learning-by-record and worker churn.
why: Skill-signaling game under AI augmentation; theoretical only.

title: The Missing Market: Diagnosing Institutional Absence in Investment Ecosystems
abstract: Why do pension funds not invest in nature? Why is human capital not an investable asset class? Why is AI 'compute' not yet a financialized commodity market? We examine why seemingly attractive investment opportunities, where the supply and demand forces are validated and underlying economics are well-understood, still fail to become recognizable, mature financial geographies. Existing scholarship on path dependence, institutional change, and evolutionary economic geography offers powerful explanations for why change does or does not occur within historically structured trajectories. However, these frameworks are less well suited to explaining "nothingness": cases in which financial markets, exchanges, or ecosystems do not emerge despite expectations that they will. This paper develops a methodological framework for studying 'nothingness'; that is, a framework for diagnosing asset-class non-consolidation within institutional investment ecosystems. The framework organizes diagnosis across three analytically distinct levels (macro-level institutions and regulation, meso-level market formation, and micro-level firm organization) and introduces porosities and blocks as the mechanisms through which practices, claims, and knowledge either translate successfully across level boundaries or fail to gain recognition and traction. Building on this framework, the paper proposes a diagnostic instrument that classifies conditions across the three levels at a given point in time, generating twenty-seven possible configurations, each linked to a recommended course of action ranging from active adoption to withdrawal. A five-step empirical protocol operationalizes the framework for practical application. The instrument offers a snapshot diagnostic: a structured way for researchers, regulators, and market actors to identify whether non-emergence is rooted in macro-level constraints, meso-level market dynamics, micro-level organizational capacity, or insufficient translation between levels, and help to determine where targeted intervention would be most effective. We illustrate the framework and instrument through a case study of US climate infrastructure.
why: Diagnosis of missing investment markets; no solution proposed.

title: Structural Financial Counterfactual Explanations for AI-driven Portfolio Allocation
abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly important in quantitative portfolio management, enabling deep learning models to capture complex nonlinear relationships between macroeconomic conditions and asset allocation decisions. Despite their predictive capability, these models often operate as black boxes, limiting transparency and reducing practitioner trust in high-stakes financial decision-making. Counterfactual explanations provide an attractive mechanism for explaining model behavior by identifying minimal input modifications that alter model predictions. However, existing counterfactual generation methods typically optimize over unrestricted feature spaces, frequently producing economically implausible market scenarios that lack practical value for institutional portfolio management. This paper proposes a financially constrained counterfactual explanation framework for AI-driven portfolio allocation. Counterfactual generation is formulated as a constrained optimization problem over economically actionable macro-financial variables while enforcing historical feasibility throughout the optimization process. Unlike unconstrained optimization, the proposed framework restricts interventions to the Federal Funds Rate, Yield Curve Slope, and market volatility, generating economically meaningful explanations that remain consistent with historically observed market behavior. Experiments conducted on 934 out-of-sample historical market observations demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially reduces intervention dimensionality relative to unconstrained counterfactual generation. Compared with an unconstrained gradientbased optimizer, the proposed approach reduces the average number of modified variables from 9.73 to 3.00, while the counterfactual success rate decreases from 57.17% to 19.27%. An ablation study further demonstrates that jointly optimizing multiple macro-financial variables substantially improves feasible recourse relative to singlevariable interventions. The results highlight the trade-off between optimization flexibility and financial realism and demonstrate the importance of incorporating domain constraints into counterfactual explanations for quantitative portfolio management.
why: Explainable portfolio AI via constrained counterfactuals; unvalidated.

title: AI Tokenomics: Pricing and Application Discovery in Foundation-Model Markets
abstract: Foundation-model providers observe rich usage histories and sell technologically distinct tokens to users running heterogeneous and expanding applications. Users choose tasks involving model-and workflow-specific token recipes predicted imperfectly beforehand, whereas application purpose, prototype success, and downstream revenue remain difficult to contract on directly. I characterize the joint determination of optimal token menu, limits to price discrimination, application discovery, and market organization, to inform platform design, enterprise procurement, and policy. The same menu governing both current and prospective applications renders discovery dependent on the density of marginally profitable applications and the metered share of development costs. Varying application populations alters optimal prices and billing dimensions, which in turn shifts the direction of discovery. Better token-consumption forecasts disproportionately encourage experimentation under uncertain prototype costs. Competition lowers markups for portable applications but limits providers' ability to recoup discovery investments.
why: Foundation-model pricing economy; tangential to financial research.

title: Generative AI Service Outages and Price Impact in Cryptocurrency Markets
abstract: Generative AI has become part of the financial information infrastructure, yet its role in shaping the functioning of capital markets remains poorly understood. We examine 252 service outages identified from the status pages of OpenAI and Anthropic and align their onset times with high-frequency Binance data for Bitcoin and Ethereum.Using a stacked difference-in-differences design, we compare market conditions before and after each outage with those on historical control days matched by weekday and UTC time. Within 15 minutes of outage onset, Amihud illiquidity and the trading-value-scaled price range decline by 15.88\% and 10.87\%, respectively, relative to their counterfactual levels. The decomposition yields point estimates consistent with both narrower price movements and greater trading value. Spot Kyle $\lambda$ falls, while directional order flow and visible depth in perpetual-contract order books do not change significantly. The response is concentrated in ETH, remains robust to alternative specifications and finite-sample inference, and does not differ systematically across providers.
why: AI outages correlate with crypto illiquidity; mechanism unclear.

title: Official Monetary Policy Narratives and Bond Risk Premia: Evidence from LLM-Based News Measures
abstract: Central bank communication and official policy narratives are critical for monetary transmission, but few studies quantify their forward-looking information in bond markets. We build an article-level Official Monetary Policy Action Score (OMPAS) via LLM semantic annotation using 1.46 million Chinese official-news articles to quantify action-oriented policy narratives. We then construct the Policy Action Signal (PAS) by linking OMPAS to future policy actions. We show that PAS significantly predicts Chinese government bond excess returns beyond yield curve factors, with stronger effects on long-maturity bonds. Its persistent component forecasts lower future yields, consistent with durable easing expectations being incorporated into the yield curve. Out-of-sample forecasts and portfolio tests show that PAS delivers tangible economic value for investors. Our paper provides an auditable LLM text measurement tool and identifies an unspanned policy narrative channel shaping bond risk premia.
why: LLM policy narratives predict bond returns out-of-sample.

title: Architects Without Offices: Strategic Hybridization as a Survival Mechanism in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Economic Volatility
abstract: The architectural profession is undergoing a structural transformation driven by the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), macroeconomic volatility, and the obsolescence of the traditional studiocentered office model. This study analyzes strategic hybridization as a survival mechanism for architects, examining how integrating remote work, digital collaboration, diversified revenue streams, and flexible legal frameworks enables professional resilience in an uncertain environment. A qualitative documentary analysis was conducted, reviewing 38 high-impact academic sources, institutional reports, and professional guidelines published between 2018 and 2026. The findings reveal that hybridization operates through three synergistic dimensions: (i) operational flexibility (reduction of fixed overheads via digital workflows and outsourced staffing), (ii) technological empowerment (adoption of AI-assisted design, BIM cloud platforms, and fintech for client management), and (iii) professional reconfiguration (multi-occupational portfolios, consulting, and passive income streams). The results indicate that while hybrid models mitigate economic risks, they introduce governance challenges and require deliberate regulatory adaptation. The study concludes that strategic hybridization is not an alternative but an imperative for architectural practice, and that it demands curricular reforms in architecture education to embed business intelligence and digital literacy. This framework provides actionable guidelines for practitioners, policymakers, and educators navigating the post-pandemic, AI-augmented professional landscape.
why: Architectural workplace strategy; off-topic entirely.

title: The Weaponization of Finance How the Plumbing of Global Money Became the Front Line of Statecraft, and What the Evidence Reveals About Its Reach and Its Limits
abstract: Since February 2022, the United States and its allies have shown that they can disable an adversary's economy from the inside: freezing central-bank reserves, severing banks from dollar clearing and messaging, denying critical technology, and taxing access to their markets. This paper asks how well that power actually works. It argues that the weaponization of finance should be judged by results, not resolve, by whether a measure achieves the political change it is meant to produce, and at what cost, rather than by the determination it signals or the pain it inflicts. On that standard, the record is uncomfortable. Financial coercion is extraordinarily effective at imposing cost and denying capability, but against determined, entrenched adversaries it rarely compels the change that is usually at its stated aim, and each use spends down the trust in the dollar system on which its leverage depends. The paper analyzes the coercive toolkit as a network centrality issue, or weaponized interdependence, focusing on the 2022 freeze of Russian reserves as a key example. It also reviews post-2022 data on central-bank gold, reserve composition, and parallel payment systems, considering alternative explanations like valuation and inflation. The findings suggest gradual hedging strategies rather than an urgent move away from the dollar. It reviews the political-effectiveness record from Cuba to Iran, where a credible off-ramp proves decisive, and explains why a tool that seldom compels nonetheless persists. It then sets out how strategic goals are secured through constraint, coalitions, and the positive-sum foundations of alliances and legitimacy, including the case for arms-control-style restraint on economic coercion. Written for students of international relations and for policymakers, it closes with five tests to apply before imposing any major financial measure.
